Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 30
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Bartender
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Worst Case Rehearsal: mentally rehearse worst case scenarios to feel prepared, Avoid Open Spaces: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable, Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions
  Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Vignette:
Layla, a 30-year-old woman with a quiet intensity, carried the weight of a childhood memory that had shaped the contours of her adult life. She was only seven when the world, as she knew it, fractured. The memory was less a story she could tell and more a series of visceral sensations: the rising tension in the air, the hushed, angry words exchanged between her parents, and then, the sudden, explosive movement. Her father, his face contorted, had lunged across the small living room towards her mother. Layla remembered the sharp gasp, the sound of something hitting the wall, and the sheer terror that paralyzed her in her spot. Even now, when the memory returned, it would flood her with such an overwhelming wave of emotion that she would have to stop whatever she was doing, gasping for breath until the wave receded. She knew what had happened, the core event, but she found herself utterly unable to find words to describe it, as if the experience itself had bypassed language.

That day had left an indelible mark, sowing a deep-seated belief that people, even those closest to you, could not truly be trusted. Layla had come to believe that she couldn't rely on herself to intervene or protect, and this self-doubt gnawed at her, making her question whether she would ever do the right thing when it mattered most. This pervasive mistrust had quietly influenced her relationships, culminating in a divorce a few years prior, leaving her feeling even more isolated and vulnerable.

Her occupation as a bartender at a busy downtown establishment placed her in an environment that constantly challenged her sense of safety. The bar was an open, exposed space, and Layla felt profoundly vulnerable there. Every shift was an exercise in vigilance. A customer’s sudden reach for a drink, an abrupt turn as they ordered, or even a raised voice from across the room would immediately put her on guard, her muscles tensing, her heart quickening. She would find herself mentally rehearsing worst-case scenarios: "What if there's a fight? Where would I go? How would I protect myself?" This constant rehearsal, while exhausting, was her attempt to feel prepared, to regain a semblance of control in a world that felt fundamentally unpredictable.

Layla had developed a limited number of places where she felt truly safe, primarily her small, meticulously secured apartment. Before going to bed each night, she would repeatedly check that all doors and windows were locked, sometimes several times, the metallic click of the deadbolt a temporary balm against her anxieties. At work, she unconsciously positioned herself behind the bar, always aware of the exits, trying to keep a visual on every corner of the room. She also tried hard to control her emotions, presenting a calm, composed front to the world, fearing that any outward display of vulnerability would invite trouble or signify a loss of control she couldn't afford. This constant emotional regulation, coupled with the relentless threat monitoring, left her physically and mentally drained after every shift.

Over the weeks and months, these habits had solidified into a way of life, leaving Layla perpetually exhausted, irritable, and isolated. The daily grind of her job, while providing a necessary structure, was also a constant source of stress, a battle against her own heightened senses. The constant state of alert, the inability to relax, and the overwhelming feeling of being trapped in this cycle finally prompted her to seek help. She was tired of living in a world where every sudden movement felt like a precursor to disaster, and she desperately wanted to find a way to live without the constant fear that had become her shadow.
